unit.name: Paper 2: Christianity
unit.subtitle: Beliefs and practices of Christianity as the second religion

lessons.title: Christian Beliefs: God, Creation and Jesus
lessons.description: The Trinity, creation, the Incarnation, the last days of Jesus and salvation in Christianity.
lessons.content_html:
The Trinity: One God in Three Persons

Christianity teaches that there is one God who exists eternally as three distinct Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is the doctrine of the Trinity. The three Persons are not three separate gods (polytheism) nor three modes of one God (modalism) — they are one God in a communion of being and love.

The Nicene Creed (325/381 CE) is Christianity’s most widely accepted doctrinal statement. It confesses the Father as creator of all things, the Son as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God,” and the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life.” The Creed is used across Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant traditions, making it the closest thing to a universal Christian statement of belief.

Matthew 3:13–17 (the baptism of Jesus) shows all three Persons simultaneously: Jesus is baptised in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven — “This is my beloved Son.”

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed was agreed at Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE). It is shared by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches. Matthew 3:13–17 is the key scriptural showing of all three Persons at once.

Creation: God and the Universe

Genesis 1–3 is the foundational Christian text on creation. Genesis 1 presents creation as six days of ordered making, culminating in humanity as the pinnacle. Genesis 2 gives a second, more intimate account focused on the first humans and their relationship with God. Genesis 3 introduces the Fall.

Christians interpret Genesis in divergent ways. A literal reading takes the six days as historical days. A metaphorical reading treats Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God’s nature (creative, purposeful, benevolent) rather than a scientific sequence. John 1:1–18 adds the dimension that creation happened ‘through the Word’ — the eternal Son was the agent through whom all things were made, “and without him not one thing came into being.”

The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The Incarnation is the belief that the second Person of the Trinity, the eternal Son (the Word or Logos), became human in the person of Jesus. John 1:14 states: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us.” 1 Timothy 3:16 calls this “the mystery of our religion” — God was manifested in flesh.

The Incarnation has enormous implications. It means Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet: he is the eternal God of the universe who chose to live a human life, to suffer and die. For Christians, this act of divine self-giving is the greatest expression of God’s love.

The Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) defined Jesus as “truly God and truly man,” with two natures in one Person. Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant churches affirm this. Some liberal Protestant theologians read the Incarnation as metaphorical — describing God’s deepest engagement with humanity rather than a literal metaphysical event. The Nicene Creed is the common anchor: “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven... and was made man.”

The Last Days of Jesus

Luke 22–24 contains the account of Jesus’ last days. The sequence is: the Last Supper (Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples, saying “This is my body... this is my blood of the new covenant”); betrayal and arrest in Gethsemane; trial before the High Priest and Pilate; crucifixion on Golgotha; burial and then resurrection (the empty tomb and appearances to Mary, to the disciples on the Emmaus road, and to the eleven).

The Last Supper is the foundation of the Eucharist practised in churches today. The crucifixion and resurrection are together the central event of Christian history — the moment of salvation.

Salvation and Atonement

Salvation is the rescue of humanity from sin. Christians teach that sin — human rebellion against God’s will — separates humanity from God. Jesus’ death on the cross is understood as the means by which that separation is overcome.

Atonement theories explain how the cross achieves salvation. John 3:16 states: “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” Acts 4:8–12 records Peter asserting that “there is salvation in no one else” but Jesus Christ — a foundational claim about the uniqueness of Christ’s saving work.

Key Fact

John 3:16 — “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” — is the key salvation verse. Acts 4:8–12 — Peter declares salvation is found in Christ alone. Both are essential 5-mark source references on salvation.

Christians agree that the cross achieves salvation but differ on how. Substitutionary atonement (popular in Reformed/evangelical Christianity): Jesus took humanity’s punishment in their place. Moral influence theory (associated with liberal Protestantism): the cross demonstrates God’s love so powerfully that it draws humanity to repentance. Christus Victor (common in Orthodox thinking): Jesus defeated the powers of sin, death and evil by dying and rising. All three agree that salvation comes through Christ; they differ on the mechanism.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers a lot of ground — the Trinity, creation, Incarnation and salvation. In a 12-mark Discuss question, focus on one big idea at a time rather than listing all of them. For example: “The most important Christian belief is the Trinity” or “Salvation is only possible through Jesus Christ.” Develop both sides: those who agree (the Trinity organises all Christian theology; Acts 4:8–12 asserts Christ alone saves) and those who challenge (some liberal Christians are more pluralist; the Incarnation or resurrection may be considered more practically important). For the 5-mark Explain question, cite a specific verse: John 3:16 for salvation, John 1:14 for the Incarnation, or Matthew 3:13–17 for the Trinity. Vague references like ‘the Gospels’ do not earn the 5th mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is defined by the Nicene Creed (325/381 CE) and shown in Matthew 3:13–17; the Incarnation (John 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16) teaches that the eternal Son became fully human.
  • Christians interpret Genesis 1–3 literally or metaphorically; John 1:1–18 adds that creation occurred through the eternal Word.
  • Salvation comes through Christ alone (Acts 4:8–12; John 3:16); atonement theories differ across denominations but all ground salvation in the cross and resurrection.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Christians believe about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) God is one being in three co-equal Persons; (2) The three Persons are Father, Son and Holy Spirit; (3) The Trinity is expressed in the Nicene Creed agreed at Nicaea (325 CE). Each must be a separately identifiable point.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian beliefs about the Incarnation.
practice_questions.marks: May include: the eternal Son of God became human in Jesus; John 1:14 — 'the Word became flesh'; 1 Timothy 3:16 calls it 'the mystery of our religion'; Jesus is both fully God and fully human; the Incarnation is the basis for the Christmas celebration. Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Christians interpret the account of creation in Genesis.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Literal interpretation — some Christians, especially evangelical or fundamentalist Protestants, understand the six days as historical days; God created the universe in six 24-hour periods; this is sometimes called Young Earth Creationism; (2) Metaphorical interpretation — many mainline Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians read Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God's nature and humanity's relationship with God, rather than a scientific account; this allows compatibility with evolutionary biology. Development beyond naming the view required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about salvation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Salvation comes through Christ alone — Acts 4:8–12 records Peter stating 'there is salvation in no one else' but Jesus; (2) God's motive for salvation is love — John 3:16 teaches that God gave his only Son so that all who believe would not perish but have eternal life. The 5th mark requires a named source: Acts 4:8–12, or John 3:16.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events in Jesus' last days as recorded in Luke 22–24.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete events: (1) The Last Supper — Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples; (2) Arrest and crucifixion — betrayed by Judas, tried by Pilate, crucified at Golgotha; (3) The resurrection — the empty tomb is found by the women; the risen Jesus appears to disciples.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important Christian belief is the resurrection of Jesus.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicitly weighs; justified conclusion. FOR: without the resurrection, the cross is merely a tragic death; 1 Corinthians 15 argues 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; resurrection is the basis of Christian hope. AGAINST: the Incarnation may be considered more foundational (without it the cross has no saving significance); others argue the Trinity is the organising belief; some emphasise the teaching of Jesus (e.g. the Sermon on the Mount) as equally central to Christian identity. Named sources: Luke 24; 1 Corinthians 15; John 3:16; Acts 4:8–12. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

lessons.title: Eschatology and the Problem of Evil
lessons.description: Christian teachings on life after death across denominations, and responses to the problem of evil.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Eschatology?

Eschatology is the study of “last things” — death, judgement, and what happens after death. For Christians, eschatology is not morbid speculation but a source of hope: the belief that death is not the end, and that God will ultimately bring justice and renewal.

Resurrection, Judgement, Heaven and Hell

Most Christian traditions teach that after death, humans face judgement, and then enter either heaven or hell. Heaven is described as eternal life in the presence of God — a state of perfect joy, peace and communion with God. Hell is described as eternal separation from God. The 39 Articles of Religion (the foundational Anglican confession of faith) affirm belief in the resurrection of the body and eternal life, but do not specify the precise nature of hell. Some Christians interpret hell as eternal conscious punishment; others see it as the final annihilation of the unrepentant; still others (universalists) believe God will ultimately save all people.

2 Corinthians 5:1–10 is a key passage for Edexcel: Paul writes that believers groan in their earthly “tent” (the body), longing for a “heavenly dwelling” made by God. He says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due to us for the things done while in the body.” This passage affirms both resurrection (a new, permanent body from God) and judgement (accountability for earthly life).

Key Fact

Purgatory is the Catholic and some Orthodox teaching that souls who die in a state of imperfect holiness undergo purification before entering heaven. It is not a second chance for the unrepentant but a process of preparation for those who die in God’s grace. Most Protestant traditions (as reflected in the 39 Articles, Article XXII) reject purgatory as “a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.” This denominational divergence is directly tested in Edexcel’s question on eschatology.

The most likely comparison in the exam is Islam or Catholic Christianity. Key comparisons: Both Christianity and Islam teach bodily resurrection, final judgement, heaven (Paradise/Jannah in Islam) and hell (Jahannam). Both affirm that what happens after death is determined by one’s response to God during earthly life. Divergence 1 — Purgatory: Catholic Christianity has a doctrine of purgatory; Islam has no direct equivalent, though some scholars discuss the barzakh (an intermediate state between death and resurrection) as a period of waiting rather than purification. Divergence 2 — Nature of salvation: Christianity teaches salvation through faith in Jesus Christ (Acts 4:8–12). Islam teaches submission (islam) to Allah, with the balance of one’s deeds assessed on the Day of Judgement; there is no equivalent to the Christian doctrine of atonement through Christ’s death. Divergence 3 — The Trinity: Christian descriptions of heaven involve the beatific vision (seeing God as he is, including the Trinity); Islamic paradise does not involve a Trinitarian concept of God.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent (all-powerful) and benevolent (completely good and loving), why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil. Philosophers argue: if God were truly omnipotent, he could prevent suffering; if God were truly benevolent, he would want to prevent it; yet suffering exists. This creates a logical tension for Christian belief in God.

Christians distinguish two kinds of suffering. Moral evil (also called moral suffering) is evil caused by free human choices — war, murder, cruelty, theft. Natural evil is suffering caused by natural events — earthquakes, diseases, floods. Both challenge belief in a good God, but in different ways. Moral evil raises questions about why God gave humans free will knowing they would misuse it. Natural evil raises questions about why God designed a world that produces suffering independently of human choice.

Key Fact

Psalm 103 responds to the problem of evil with a declaration of God’s compassion: “The Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.” Christians use this Psalm to argue that God’s love and care for the suffering is itself part of the answer to the problem — God does not stand aloof but suffers with humanity (especially revealed in the incarnation and crucifixion). Psalm 119 returns repeatedly to trusting God’s word even in affliction: “It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees” — suggesting that suffering has a spiritual purpose for the believer. The book of Job is a sustained biblical engagement with the problem: Job suffers catastrophically without deserving it, protests to God, and ultimately receives not an explanation but an encounter with God’s greatness.

Solutions to the Problem of Evil

Christians offer several responses to the problem of evil. The free will defence argues that God gave humans genuine freedom, which makes moral evil a human responsibility rather than God’s. A world with free will is considered better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused. This does not fully explain natural evil, however.

COMMON EXAM ERROR: Students frequently confuse these two theodicies. They are distinct and must not be attributed to the wrong thinker. Augustine (354–430 CE): Evil is the privation (absence) of good — it has no independent existence but is what happens when goodness is removed. The cause of evil is the misuse of free will, first by Satan, then by Adam and Eve (the Fall). This is the ‘free will theodicy’ or ‘Augustinian theodicy.’ Books: City of God, Confessions. Key contrast: creation was originally ‘very good’ (Genesis 1); evil entered through human sin. Augustine does NOT use the phrase ‘soul-making.’ Irenaeus (c.130–202 CE): Humans were created immature, made in the ‘image of God’ but not yet in his ‘likeness’ — they need to grow. Evil and suffering are the necessary conditions for moral and spiritual development. Modern development: John Hick (*Evil and the God of Love*, 1966) called this the ‘soul-making theodicy’ or the ‘vale of soul-making’. The world is not a paradise but a place where souls develop through facing challenges and suffering. Key contrast with Augustine: evil is not a consequence of a past Fall but a necessary feature for human growth. NEVER attribute ‘soul-making’ to Augustine.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The Augustinian/Irenaean/Hick distinction is one of the most commonly examined misconceptions in this topic. In the exam, if asked about the ‘vale of soul-making,’ name both Irenaeus (the originator) and John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) who developed it — do NOT attribute it to Augustine. For a 5-mark question requiring a source of wisdom, you can cite Psalm 103 (“The Lord is compassionate and gracious”), Psalm 119 (“It was good for me to be afflicted”), 2 Corinthians 5:1–10, or the 39 Articles by name. On 12-mark Discuss questions about whether suffering disproves God’s existence, the strongest answers develop both the intellectual challenge (the logical problem of evil) AND at least two responses (free will, soul-making, the cross as God’s solidarity with suffering), then weigh them explicitly before concluding. SPaG: spell ‘eschatology’, ‘omnipotent’, ‘benevolent’ and ‘theodicy’ correctly for those marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christian eschatology teaches resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell; Catholics add purgatory (rejected by Protestants via the 39 Articles); 2 Corinthians 5:1–10 affirms both resurrection and judgement. Comparison point: Islam also teaches resurrection and judgement but without purgatory or atonement through Christ.
  • The problem of evil asks how an omnipotent, benevolent God can allow moral suffering (caused by human choices) and natural suffering (earthquakes, disease); Psalm 103, Psalm 119 and Job are biblical responses showing compassion, trust and encounter with God.
  • Augustine: evil as privation of good caused by the Fall and free will. Irenaeus/John Hick: the ‘vale of soul-making’ — suffering is necessary for moral/spiritual development. Never attribute soul-making to Augustine.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Christians believe in the resurrection of the body after death.
- Christians believe in a final judgement where each person faces accountability for their earthly life.
- Christians believe in heaven — eternal life in God's presence.
- Christians believe in hell — eternal separation from God.
- Catholic (and some Orthodox) Christians believe in purgatory — purification for souls not yet fully holy.
- Protestant traditions (39 Articles) reject purgatory.
Each point must be identifiably distinct — not three sentences rephrasing the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the 39 Articles of Religion teach about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- The 39 Articles affirm belief in the resurrection of the body.
- They affirm eternal life in heaven for the saved.
- Article XXII explicitly rejects purgatory as 'a fond thing vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.'
- They reflect the Protestant (Anglican) position that heaven and hell are the only post-mortem destinations.
[1 mark per accurate point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the problem of evil challenges Christian belief in God.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Moral evil (caused by human choices — war, murder, cruelty) challenges belief in an omnipotent God: if God is all-powerful, why does he allow humans to choose to harm each other? Some conclude that either God is not all-powerful, or he does not care.
- Natural evil (earthquakes, disease, floods) challenges belief in a benevolent God: unlike moral evil, natural evil cannot be blamed on human free will. A truly loving God could apparently design a world without natural disasters. Its existence seems incompatible with a creator who is both powerful and good.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- The free will defence (Augustine): God gave humans genuine freedom; moral evil is the result of that freedom being misused. God is not responsible for choices made by free creatures. A world with free will is better than a world of moral robots, even if free will is misused.
- The soul-making theodicy (Irenaeus, developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love, 1966): suffering is the necessary condition for moral and spiritual growth. The world is a 'vale of soul-making' — if everything were comfortable, humans would never develop courage, compassion or faith. Psalm 119 reflects this: 'It was good for me to be afflicted so that I might learn your decrees.'

The 5th mark: name a source — 'John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966)', 'Psalm 103', 'Psalm 119', '2 Corinthians 5:1-10', or the book of Job. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'The vale of soul-making is the most convincing Christian response to the problem of evil.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources (Hick, Augustine, scripture); explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- The soul-making theodicy explains both moral and natural evil: both are necessary conditions for humans to develop virtues like courage, compassion and faith. It is more comprehensive than the free will defence, which only addresses moral evil.
- John Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966) grounds soul-making in Irenaeus's theology (c.130-202 CE) — the idea that humans are created immature and grow towards 'the likeness of God.' This gives the theodicy deep roots in Christian tradition, not just modern philosophy.
- The Bible supports the idea that suffering has a developmental purpose: Psalm 119 states 'It was good for me to be afflicted'; the book of Job ends not with an explanation of Job's suffering but with his deepened encounter with God.

Arguments against:
- The soul-making theodicy struggles with extreme suffering (Holocaust, childhood cancer) that goes far beyond any plausible 'educational' purpose. John Hick himself acknowledged this weakness. A child who dies in agony before developing moral character cannot easily be said to have 'benefited' from suffering.
- Augustine's free will defence has strong scriptural grounding in the Fall narrative (Genesis 3) and Paul's teaching on original sin. For many Christians this is more convincing because it identifies a cause of evil (human rebellion) rather than asking victims to find meaning in their pain.
- Non-religious critics argue that both theodicies are post-hoc rationalisations — invented to protect belief in God rather than genuine explanations. The problem of evil, they argue, gives good reason to conclude there is no God.
- Both theodicies leave natural evil partially unexplained. If God could have made a world without earthquakes or disease but chose not to, soul-making does not fully answer why.

SPaG: 'theodicy', 'eschatology', 'omnipotent', 'benevolent' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Christian and Islamic beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that after death all people will face judgement by God: Christians believe they will appear before 'the judgment seat of Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:10); Muslims believe their deeds will be weighed on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).
- Both Christianity and Islam teach that the outcome of judgement is either heaven or hell: Christians describe heaven as eternal life in God's presence; Islamic teaching describes Paradise (Jannah) as a state of joy and divine favour. Both traditions describe hell as a place of punishment for the unrepentant.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

lessons.title: Christian Worship, Sacraments and Prayer
lessons.description: Liturgical and non-liturgical worship, sacraments across denominations, and the nature of prayer.
lessons.content_html:
Forms of Christian Worship

Worship is how Christians express love and devotion to God. Christians worship in several distinct forms, and different denominations emphasise different approaches.

Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure. Anglican services follow the Book of Common Prayer (or its modern successor, Common Worship); Catholic services follow the Roman Rite; Orthodox services follow centuries-old liturgical patterns. The advantage is that worshippers know what to expect, the service connects them to centuries of Christian tradition, and the same words unite Christians globally. Anglicans, Catholics and Orthodox all use liturgical worship as their primary form.

Non-liturgical worship is less structured and more flexible. It is common in Methodist, Baptist and many Reformed churches. There is no prescribed prayer book; sermons are central; hymns and readings are chosen to suit the congregation’s needs. Some Christians prefer this form because it allows the Spirit to guide the service rather than following a predetermined script.

Key Fact

The Book of Common Prayer (1662 version) is the historical service book of the Church of England, providing set liturgies for Morning Prayer, Evening Prayer, Holy Communion and other rites. It shaped Anglican worship for centuries and remains in use today, especially in traditional parish churches. Many Anglicans also use the modern Common Worship (2000) book. Knowing its name and denominational context is important for exam questions.

Pentecostal churches (and charismatic congregations in other denominations) worship very differently from liturgical traditions. Services are spontaneous and led by the Spirit: worship includes contemporary music with guitars, drums and clapping; congregants may speak in tongues (glossolalia), give prophecies, pray aloud spontaneously and respond physically. There is no fixed order of service and no prayer book. Pentecostal worship has grown rapidly in the UK and globally — it is the fastest-growing Christian expression worldwide. The contrast between Pentecostal and Anglican/Catholic liturgical worship is a prime example for exam questions on denominational diversity.

The most common exam comparison is with Islam. Similarities: Both Christian and Islamic worship include communal prayer, reading from sacred scripture, and acts of praise directed towards God. Friday Jumu'ah prayers in Islam and Sunday services in Christianity both serve as the primary communal worship event of the week. Differences: Islamic Salah is highly ritualised (five set times daily, specific bodily postures, Arabic recitation, ritual purity required); Christian worship varies enormously from the Pentecostal free-flowing to the Catholic Mass. Islamic worship is strictly non-sacramental; Christian worship often centres on sacramental acts (Eucharist, baptism). Islam explicitly rejects the use of music and images in worship in many traditions; Christianity has a rich tradition of sacred music and art.

Sacraments in Different Denominations

A sacrament is an outward, visible sign of an inward, spiritual reality. The number of sacraments is a significant denominational difference. Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance (Reconciliation), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony. Most Protestant churches recognise only two — Baptism and the Eucharist (Lord’s Supper) — because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels. The 39 Articles XXV–XXXVI are the Anglican doctrinal statement on sacraments: Article XXV affirms two sacraments “ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel” (Baptism and the Supper of the Lord) and describes the five other Catholic sacraments as “not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel.”

Baptism is the sacrament of initiation into the Christian community — widely practised across denominations. The mode and timing vary: Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox baptise infants (paedo-baptism); Baptists and many evangelicals baptise only those who have made a personal declaration of faith (believer’s baptism). The meaning also varies: in Catholic and Orthodox theology, baptism washes away original sin and incorporates the person into the Body of Christ; in Protestant theology, it is primarily a sign of inclusion in the covenant community and a declaration of faith.

The Eucharist (also called Holy Communion, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) is the other universally accepted sacrament. However, what happens during the Eucharist is one of Christianity’s most significant theological disputes. Catholics teach transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine is truly transformed into the body and blood of Christ, though the outward appearance remains. Most Protestants either hold a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only, recalling Christ’s sacrifice) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is genuinely but spiritually present in the sharing). The Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles deliberately leave room for both views.

Prayer: Set and Informal

Prayer is a central Christian practice. Jesus taught about prayer in Matthew 6:5–14: he warned against ostentatious public praying done to impress others, and instructed his followers to pray in private and to use a model he gave them — the Lord’s Prayer. Christians use two main types of prayer. Set prayers are written texts used repeatedly — for example, the Lord’s Prayer, the General Confession from the Book of Common Prayer, or prayers from liturgical books. They provide unity, connect worshippers to tradition, and are especially central in liturgical worship. Informal prayer uses the believer’s own words, allowing personal and spontaneous expression of faith.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) is the model prayer Jesus gave his disciples. It is the one prayer shared by virtually all Christian denominations worldwide, said in liturgical services, at weddings, baptisms and funerals. Its structure includes: address to God as Father in heaven; hallowing of his name (praise); petition for God’s kingdom to come; request for daily bread (provision); request for forgiveness; and protection from temptation and evil. It teaches Christians that prayer should combine praise, submission to God’s will, requests for daily needs and forgiveness.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Worship (2.1*) is a starred comparison point — in a 12-mark Discuss question you may be asked to compare Christian worship with that of another religion. Always develop both sides: “Christians … [named denomination + source]; in contrast, Muslims ….” For a 5-mark source question on prayer, the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:5–14) and the Book of Common Prayer are both named Edexcel sources — either earns the 5th mark if properly attributed and developed. The most common student error on sacraments questions is stating only that “Catholics have seven and Protestants have two” without developing why Protestants reduced the number (only baptism and Eucharist were commanded by Jesus in the Gospels) or what the 39 Articles say specifically. SPaG marks: ‘Eucharist’, ‘liturgical’, ‘sacrament’ and ‘Pentecostal’ are high-value specialist terms — spell them correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christian worship ranges from liturgical (fixed structure, Book of Common Prayer, Catholic Mass) to non-liturgical (flexible, Bible-centred) to Pentecostal (spontaneous, Spirit-led) — this spec point is starred (2.1*) requiring comparison with another religion such as Islam.
  • Most Protestant churches recognise two sacraments (Baptism and Eucharist, as commanded by Jesus — 39 Articles XXV); Catholics and Orthodox recognise seven; key Eucharist difference: Catholics teach transubstantiation, most Protestants hold a memorialist or spiritual-presence view.
  • Prayer includes set prayers (e.g. the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:9-13) and informal prayer; Jesus taught that prayer should combine praise, submission, request and forgiveness, and warned against ostentatious displays (Matthew 6:5).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of liturgical Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure (set prayers, set responses).
- It is used by Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
- The Book of Common Prayer (Anglican) or Roman Rite (Catholic) provides the set texts.
- A minister or priest leads the congregation through the set order.
- The Eucharist/Mass is typically central to liturgical worship.
Do not award marks for three sentences that elaborate the same point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how Pentecostal Christians worship differently from Anglican Christians.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Pentecostal worship is spontaneous and led by the Holy Spirit; there is no fixed order of service or prayer book.
- It may include speaking in tongues (glossolalia), prophecy, healing prayer and contemporary music with guitars and clapping.
- Anglican worship is liturgical — following the set structure of the Book of Common Prayer or Common Worship, with set prayers and responses led by a minister.
[1 mark per accurate contrasting point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian beliefs about sacraments differ between denominations.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Catholics and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments; most Protestant traditions (including Anglicans, as stated in the 39 Articles XXV) recognise only two — baptism and the Eucharist. Protestants reduced the number because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels; the five Catholic sacraments are described in the 39 Articles as not being 'Sacraments of the Gospel.'
- The meaning of the Eucharist differs significantly: Catholics teach transubstantiation — the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (the outward appearance remains but the substance changes). Most Protestant Christians hold either a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is spiritually but not physically present). This is one of the most significant points of division in the Reformation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians use set prayers, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Set prayers connect Christians to centuries of tradition and unite believers across denominations: the Lord's Prayer is said in virtually all Christian services worldwide, from Catholic Mass to Baptist Sunday worship. Matthew 6:9-13 records Jesus specifically teaching this prayer to his disciples as a model — its regular use keeps Christians grounded in the pattern Jesus himself gave.
- Set prayers provide a reliable structure for worship, especially for those who struggle to find words: the Book of Common Prayer gives worshippers tested, beautiful language for confession, thanksgiving and praise. Using the same words as Christians across generations creates a sense of continuity with the historic Church.

The 5th mark: name a specific source — 'Matthew 6:9-13 (the Lord's Prayer)', 'the Book of Common Prayer' or another clearly identified text. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Liturgical worship is more important than informal worship for Christians today.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a shared structure that unites the Church globally: the same Eucharistic prayers, the same Lord's Prayer, the same lectionary readings unite Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox across the world. The Book of Common Prayer has shaped English-speaking Christianity for over 350 years.
- Liturgical worship is ordered and biblical: set scripture readings, the Nicene Creed and the Lord's Prayer ensure that core doctrine and key texts are rehearsed regularly. This guards against theological drift and ensures worshippers are formed by the whole of Scripture, not just a preacher's preferences.
- Sacraments (central to liturgical worship) are considered by Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican Christians to be genuine channels of God's grace — not symbolic but effective. Without sacramental worship, Christians may miss out on the grace God intends to give through these means.

Arguments against:
- Pentecostal and charismatic worship has grown fastest globally, suggesting that many Christians find less structured, Spirit-led worship more meaningful and life-giving. Jesus himself warned against empty, repetitive prayer (Matthew 6:7 — 'do not keep on babbling'); liturgical services can become mechanical.
- Informal prayer allows Christians to bring their personal concerns before God in their own words: Jesus encouraged private, personal prayer in Matthew 6:6 ('go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen'). Formal liturgy cannot always meet the individual's specific spiritual needs.
- Many Baptist, Methodist and evangelical Christians argue that the New Testament church was not liturgical in the Catholic sense: the emphasis in the early Church was on preaching, communal prayer and breaking of bread in simple settings, not an elaborate ritual structure.

SPaG: 'liturgical', 'Eucharist', 'sacrament', 'Pentecostal' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic approaches to baptism.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The timing of baptism differs: Catholics (and Anglicans, Orthodox) practise infant baptism (paedo-baptism), baptising babies into the community of faith, believing it removes original sin and incorporates the child into the Body of Christ. Baptists and many evangelicals practise believer's baptism — only those who have personally declared faith in Jesus are baptised, because it is seen as a public expression of individual faith.
- The theological meaning differs: in Catholic theology, baptism is a sacrament that confers grace, washes away original sin and makes the person a member of the Church. In Baptist theology, baptism is an ordinance — an act of obedience that publicly expresses a faith already present in the believer's heart. Grace is received through faith, not through the water of baptism.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

glossary_terms.definition: Acts of praise, honour and devotion directed towards God, either collectively or individually.
A church service that follows a set, formal structure with prescribed prayers and responses, often using a service book.
A church service without a fixed, written order — the minister has flexibility in how the service is structured.
A charismatic Christian denomination emphasising the direct experience of the Holy Spirit through speaking in tongues, healing, prophecy and spontaneous worship.

lessons.title: Pilgrimage, Festivals, Mission and the Worldwide Church
lessons.description: Christian pilgrimage sites, Christmas and Easter, mission, and the worldwide Church.
lessons.content_html:
Christian Pilgrimage

Pilgrimage is a journey made to a sacred place for spiritual reasons. Christians have practised pilgrimage since the earliest centuries. The spec names four sites:

  • Jerusalem: The holiest site in Christianity, where Jesus was crucified, buried and raised. Pilgrims visit the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the Via Dolorosa and the Garden of Gethsemane. Jerusalem is also holy to Jews and Muslims, making it a place of both spiritual depth and ongoing geo-political complexity.
  • Iona (Scotland): A small island off the west coast of Scotland where St Columba founded a monastery in 563 CE. The Iona Community (founded 1938 by George MacLeod) has made it a centre of ecumenical spirituality and social justice Christianity. Pilgrims come for retreat, reflection and the experience of Celtic spirituality.
  • Taizé (France): An ecumenical community founded in 1940 by Brother Roger Schutz. Each year tens of thousands of young people from across the world visit Taizé for prayer, song and reconciliation. Its simple, repetitive chants have become widely used across denominations. Taizé emphasises unity between Catholics and Protestants.
  • Walsingham (England): England’s national Marian shrine, dating to 1061. After destruction at the Reformation, it was restored in the twentieth century and is now visited by both Catholics and Anglicans. It represents the healing of divisions between denominations.

Luke 2:41–43 provides a biblical basis for pilgrimage: the young Jesus goes with his parents to Jerusalem for the Passover, showing that visiting sacred sites is part of faithful Jewish (and, by extension, Christian) practice.

Catholics and Orthodox strongly affirm pilgrimage as spiritually meritorious. Protestant reformers (Luther, Calvin) were more cautious: they rejected the idea that visiting a physical location earns spiritual credit, arguing God is present everywhere. Modern Protestants vary: some travel to Israel for educational reasons without claiming spiritual merit; others, like those visiting Iona or Taizé, do so for community and renewal rather than indulgences.

Christian Festivals: Christmas and Easter

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human in Jesus. The liturgical season of Advent begins four Sundays before Christmas and is a time of spiritual preparation and expectation. Christmas Day (25 December in Western churches) celebrates the birth of Jesus. The Christmas story combines Matthew 2 (Magi, Herod, Egypt) and Luke 2 (shepherds, manger, Bethlehem).

Easter is the most important Christian festival, celebrating Christ’s resurrection. It is preceded by Holy Week: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem), Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, washing of feet), Good Friday (crucifixion), Holy Saturday (the waiting), Easter Sunday (resurrection).

1 Corinthians 15:12–34 is Paul’s great defence of the resurrection: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.” Paul argues the entire Christian hope rests on the historical reality of the resurrection. Without it, Christianity collapses.

Key Fact

1 Corinthians 15:12–34: Paul argues that if Christ has not been raised, faith is “futile.” The resurrection of Jesus is the guarantee of Christians’ own future resurrection. Easter celebrates this as historical fact, not symbol.

Mission, Evangelism and the Future of the Church

Mission is the Church’s outward movement into the world. Evangelism is the direct proclamation of the Gospel. Mark 16:9–20 (the so-called ‘longer ending’) records the risen Jesus commissioning his disciples: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” The spec includes this as the basis for Christian missionary work.

The Local and Worldwide Church

The local church serves its immediate community. This includes: regular Sunday worship as the centre of Christian identity; outreach work (food banks, community cafes, debt counselling); ecumenism (working across denominations in shared projects); and pastoral care for individuals.

The worldwide Church works for reconciliation and supports persecuted Christians. Christian Aid is the named development agency in this spec. It works in partnership with local organisations across the Global South on relief and development, grounded in Matthew 25:31–46 (the Sheep and Goats): Christians are called to see Christ in “the least of these.”

Key Fact

Christian Aid operates in over 40 countries, tackling poverty through long-term development. Its work is grounded in Matthew 25:31–46. The local church’s community role includes food banks, outreach work and ecumenical partnerships.

These two sites are Edexcel-specific pilgrimage sites not commonly found in other GCSE specifications. Iona is significant as the birthplace of Scottish Christianity and a centre of Celtic spirituality and social justice. Taizé is significant as an ecumenical community drawing hundreds of thousands of young Christians annually, representing hope for unity between Catholic and Protestant churches. Both are alternatives to the traditional ‘relic-and-indulgence’ model of pilgrimage — their significance is more about community and spiritual renewal than seeking miraculous healing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Iona and Taizé are Edexcel-specific sites — know what makes each distinctive (Iona: Celtic spirituality, social justice, founded by Columba 563 CE; Taizé: ecumenical, Brother Roger 1940, young people, unity). For the 12-mark Discuss on mission: “The most important work of the Christian Church is mission and evangelism.” Develop for (the Great Commission; 1 Corinthians 15 ties everything to resurrection and proclamation) and against (social action is equally important; Matthew 25 says serving the poor is serving Christ; Christian Aid’s development work is mission without words). The 5-mark Explain question on Easter should cite 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 specifically — that is the named scripture anchor for why the resurrection matters to Christians. ‘Ecumenism’ and ‘evangelism’ are examinable technical terms — spelling them correctly earns SPaG marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four spec pilgrimage sites are Jerusalem, Iona (Celtic spirituality), Taizé (ecumenical unity) and Walsingham (Marian, Catholic/Anglican); Luke 2:41–43 provides the biblical basis.
  • Easter is the central Christian festival celebrating the resurrection; 1 Corinthians 15:12–34 argues the resurrection is the foundation of all Christian hope.
  • Mission and evangelism (Mark 16:9–20) and care for the poor (Christian Aid; Matthew 25:31–46) are the two main expressions of the Church’s worldwide calling.

practice_questions.text: Outline three reasons why Christians go on pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) To deepen faith by visiting the places where Jesus lived and died (Jerusalem); (2) For spiritual renewal and community (Iona, Taize); (3) As an act of penance, thanksgiving or seeking healing (Walsingham, Lourdes). Three separately identifiable reasons.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians celebrate during Holy Week.
practice_questions.marks: May include: Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem); Maundy Thursday (Last Supper, foot washing); Good Friday (crucifixion and death of Jesus); Holy Saturday (waiting); Easter Sunday (resurrection celebrated). Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways the local church serves its community.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Outreach work — local churches run food banks, debt counselling and community cafes, meeting practical needs in their area and putting Matthew 25 into practice; (2) Ecumenical partnership — local churches of different denominations work together on shared projects, expressing the prayer of Jesus for unity in John 17:21. Development required beyond naming the activity.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Easter is the most important Christian festival, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Easter celebrates the resurrection, which Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:17 calls the basis of all Christian faith — 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; (2) Easter marks the defeat of sin and death — it is the moment when Christ's atoning work on the cross is vindicated, giving Christians hope of their own resurrection. 5th mark requires a named source: 1 Corinthians 15:12–34.

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between pilgrimage to Iona and pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points: (1) Jerusalem is the site of Jesus' death and resurrection — the most historically significant Christian site; Iona is a site of Celtic spirituality and social justice without direct gospel-history significance; (2) Jerusalem is shared by Christians, Jews and Muslims and has geopolitical complexity; Iona is a quieter, retreat-focused community site; (3) Jerusalem pilgrimage is ancient; Iona Community was founded in 1938 by George MacLeod.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important work of the worldwide Church is evangelism.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed, named sources, explicit weighing, justified conclusion. FOR: the Great Commission (Mark 16:9–20) instructs disciples to 'go into all the world and proclaim the good news'; 1 Corinthians 15 shows the resurrection must be proclaimed; without evangelism the Church shrinks and cannot fulfil its purpose. AGAINST: Matthew 25:31–46 teaches that serving 'the least of these' is serving Christ — development work (Christian Aid) is equally central; actions speak louder than words; some argue that justice and reconciliation are the primary mission. Named sources: Mark 16:9–20; 1 Corinthians 15; Matthew 25:31–46. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

The four-week period of preparation and expectation before Christmas, beginning four Sundays before 25 December.
The final week of Lent, beginning on Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem) and ending on Easter Sunday, encompassing the events of Jesus' passion.
The Church's calling to spread the Gospel throughout the world, making disciples of all nations.
The specific act of proclaiming the Christian Gospel to those who have not yet heard or believed it, with the aim of making converts.
The movement for the visible unity of different Christian denominations, expressing the prayer of Jesus in John 17:21 that his followers 'may be one.'
